title: What is alive?
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Biology Unit 1.1 'Animals and plants alive!' (living, once living and never living; animals and plants are both alive). No textbook needed.
summary: A dry seed does not move, eat or grow. Is it alive? Your child sorts things into alive, once alive and never alive, and finds that some are hard to place. They wake sleeping seeds with water, watch yeast blow up a balloon, and find the signs of life in a potted plant, an ant and themselves. They find that every living thing needs water, air and food, and meet a date palm who grew from a seed 2,000 years old.
subconcepts: alive, once alive and never alive
signs living things show: growing, feeding, drinking, breathing, moving or responding, making young
plants are alive too, in a slower way
a seed is a sleeping baby plant (dormant)
waking a seed needs water and warmth (germination)
living things can die and then can't wake again
tiny living things too small to see (yeast, microbes)
once-alive materials at home: wood, cotton, paper, silk, wool, leather
all living things need water, air and food
living things make young like themselves
living things depend on non-living things (sun, water, soil, air)
humans are one kind of living thing among millions
tiny living things live in and on your body
builds_on: This is the first time. In Class 3 your child comes back to the question with the seven signs scientists use (MRS GREN), cells, harder cases (fire, crystals, viruses, robots) and the environment. In Class 5, microorganisms and how life began.
goals: By the end your child can sort things into alive, once alive and never alive, and give a reason for each.
By the end your child can name what living things do: grow, need food, water and air, breathe, move or respond, and make young.
By the end your child can show that a seed is alive even though the seed looks dead, by making the seed grow, and say what wakes a seed.
By the end your child can say that animals and plants are both alive, even though plants don't walk.
By the end your child can find once-alive things in their own home and say what living thing they came from.
By the end your child can ask 'how do you know?' about whether something is alive.
words: able to grow, feed, breathe, respond to the world and make young
was part of something alive but isn't any more, like wood or a dry leaf
was never alive, like a stone, glass or steel
a baby plant inside a hard coat, with food stored for when they start to grow
alive but resting, not growing, waiting for water and warmth
when a seed wakes up and starts to grow a root and a shoot
tiny living things, too small to see one by one, that make dough and idli batter rise
the babies of a living thing
the things a living thing must have to stay alive: water, air and food

days.title: Alive, or not?
days.goal: Sort things and argue about the tricky ones.

steps.title: The mystery bag
steps.do: Put these in a bag: a stone, a dry bean (rajma or karamani), a dry leaf, a wooden spoon, a toy car, a banana, a piece of coconut shell and a small packet of dry yeast. Pull out one thing at a time. Your child says 'alive', 'not alive' or 'not sure', and why. Don't correct anything yet. Just say: 'Interesting. Let's find out.'

steps.title: Sort into three
steps.do: Make three circles on the floor with string or chalk: 'alive', 'once alive' and 'never alive'. Say: 'Once alive means it was part of a living thing, but isn't now.' Sort the things together. The wooden spoon was part of a tree. The coconut shell was part of a coconut palm. Put the bean and the yeast in a 'not sure' pile: this week you will test them. Then do sections A and B of Worksheet ws1. Read each word aloud and your child taps the right box.

steps.title: How do you know?
steps.do: Point to each thing in 'alive' and ask: 'How do you know it's alive?' Write the reasons on a big sheet: it grows, it eats, it drinks, it breathes, it moves by itself, it has babies. Read the list back. This is your 'signs of life' sheet. Stick it on the wall for the week. Ask: 'Do you show these signs?' (Yes: you grow, eat, drink, breathe and move.) Say: 'So you are a living thing. There are millions of kinds of living things on Earth, and you are one of them.'

need: a bag with a stone, a dry bean, a dry leaf, a wooden spoon, a toy car, a banana, a piece of coconut shell and a packet of dry yeast

days.title: Is a seed alive?
days.goal: Test the 'not sure' pile: can a seed wake up?

steps.title: Seed detectives
steps.do: Look closely at a dry rajma bean, with a hand lens if you have one. Ask: 'Does the bean breathe? Move? Eat? Grow?' Most children say no. Ask: 'So is the bean alive?' Write your child's answer on the signs sheet with today's date, so you can check it later.

steps.title: Wake the seeds
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: soaked beans on damp cotton, dry beans on dry cotton, and boiled beans on damp cotton. First ask: 'Which beans will grow? Why do you think so?' Your child draws the three cups. Then say: 'A seed that is alive but resting is called dormant. When a seed wakes up and starts to grow, we say it germinates.'

steps.title: Dance: wake like a seed
steps.do: Your child curls up tight on the floor like a dry seed, still and quiet. You are the rain. Sprinkle your fingers over them and say 'water, warmth'. Slowly they push out one foot (the root, going down), then an arm (the shoot, going up), then stand up tall. Ask: 'When you were curled up, were you alive?' (Yes, just resting.)

steps.title: Story: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Then ask the 'Talk about it' questions. Listen for: 'The baby palm was inside the seed all along' and 'The water woke the seed up.'

need: rajma or other big beans (karamani or mochai work too)
a hand lens if you have one
a few beans boiled by a grown-up

prep.task: Soak 3 beans in water overnight. Boil 3 more for 10 minutes and let them cool.

days.title: Plants are alive too
days.goal: Find signs of life at home and see that plants are alive too.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the three seed cups. Are the soaked beans fatter? Has a skin split? Your child draws what they see. Keep cups A and C damp.

steps.title: Signs of life hunt at home
steps.do: Do the hunt in Worksheet ws2, at home and at the window. Find something growing (a new leaf on a potted plant), breathing (watch your own chest, or a pet), eating (ants carrying a crumb, a crow pecking at the window), moving by itself, with babies or eggs (a pigeon's nest on a ledge, or a picture), once alive and never alive. Look at nests, but never touch. Your child ticks or draws each one. If you have a garden or a park nearby, do the hunt there too.

steps.title: Is a tree alive?
steps.do: Stand by a potted plant. Ask: 'Is this plant alive? Plants don't walk or eat like us.' Go through the signs sheet. Do plants grow? (Yes: new leaves come and they get taller.) Drink? (Their roots take in water from the soil.) Eat? (They make their own food in their green leaves, using sunlight.) Breathe? (Through tiny holes in their leaves.) Move? (Slowly: leaves turn towards the light, and flowers open and close.) Make young? (Yes, seeds.) Say: 'Plants and animals are both alive. Plants just do most things more slowly.'

days.title: Tiny life wakes up
days.goal: See that some living things are too small to see.

steps.title: Seed check and the cloth-seller
steps.do: Look at the seed cups and draw them. Then tell your child about voice v2: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth-seller with no university degree. He made his own tiny glass lenses and was the first person to see living things too small for our eyes. Ask: 'Why do you think the experts did not believe him at first?'

steps.title: The balloon that blows itself up
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 with yeast, sugar, warm water and a balloon. While you wait, ask: 'Yeast looks like brown sand. Is sand alive? What would yeast have to do to show us it is alive?' (Grow, eat, breathe, make more yeast.) When the balloon fills, say: 'Yeast is millions of tiny living things. They were dormant, like the seeds. Warm water woke them up. They ate the sugar and gave out a gas, and the gas filled the balloon.' Move the yeast from 'not sure' to 'alive'.

steps.title: Alive or Not? card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Sort the cards into alive, once alive and never alive. Every time someone places a card, the others may ask: 'How do you know?'

days.title: Once alive, all around the house
days.goal: Find things in the home that were once part of living things.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the seed cups. By now a white root has often come out of the soaked beans. Ask: 'Which way is the root growing?' (Down.) 'Have the boiled beans done anything?' (No.) Your child draws it.

steps.title: Once-alive treasure hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Your child finds 10 things at home that were once part of a living thing, and says which living thing each came from. For example: a wooden chair (a tree), a cotton veshti or kurta (the cotton plant), a newspaper (trees), a silk saree (silkworms), a woollen shawl (sheep), a jute bag (the jute plant), a coconut shell (a coconut palm), honey (made by bees from flowers), rice and dal (plants). Ask: 'Is most of our food once alive?' (Yes. Nearly all of it, except salt and water.)

steps.title: Babies like their parents
steps.do: Name a mother animal and your child names the baby: cow and calf, hen and chick, dog and puppy, cat and kitten, goat and kid, frog and tadpole, butterfly and caterpillar, a woman and her baby. Ask: 'Does a mango seed grow into a coconut tree?' (No, into a mango tree.) 'Does a stone have babies? Does a toy?' Say: 'Living things make young like themselves. Never-alive things can't.' Do section C of Worksheet ws1.

need: a basket for the treasure hunt

days.title: What every living thing needs
days.goal: See that living things need water, air and food, and depend on non-living things.

steps.title: The boiled seeds
steps.do: Look at the seed cups. The soaked beans have roots and maybe a shoot. The dry beans have not changed: they are still dormant. The boiled beans never grew. Ask gently: 'Why didn't the boiled beans grow?' (Boiling killed the baby plant inside. A living thing that has died can't wake up again.) Now put the dry beans on damp cotton too, and look again tomorrow.

steps.title: Needs, not wants
steps.do: Ask: 'What do you need to stay alive?' Help your child sort the ideas into needs (water, air, food, a safe place, sleep) and wants (a toy, TV, sweets). Ask the same for a crow (water, air, food, a tree to nest in), a tulsi plant (water, air, sunlight, soil) and the yeast (water, warmth, sugar). Say: 'Every living thing needs water, air and food. Water, air, sunlight and soil are not alive. So living things need non-living things.' Your child draws a plant in the middle of a page, with arrows to it from the Sun, a cloud, the air and the soil. Then say: 'Tiny living things called bacteria live in and on your body. There are about as many of them as there are cells in your body, and many help you digest your food.'

steps.title: Voice v1 and the project
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1. Sarah Sallon asked if 2,000-year-old date seeds might still be alive, and the plant scientist Elaine Solowey planted them. One sprouted. Ask: 'Can something be alive and look completely dead?' Then start the project. Your child divides a tray into three with paper strips and starts collecting things for the 'alive museum': a seedling from the cups, a feather, a stone, a coin.

days.title: The museum opens
days.goal: Show what you know and wonder about the hard cases.

steps.title: Finish the museum
steps.do: Finish the project tray: alive, once alive and never alive, with 3 to 5 things in each. Your child says a label for each and you write it: 'Feather. Once alive. It came from a pigeon.' Put a sprouting bean from the cups in the 'alive' section.

steps.title: Hard cases
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 together. Read each question aloud and write your child's words. Then ask: 'Is fire alive? Fire grows, moves, needs air and burns wood.' 'Is a cloud alive?' After each answer ask: 'How could we find out?' Say: 'Scientists still argue about some hard cases. You will meet them again in Class 3.'

steps.title: Museum tour and teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the museum guide for the family and explains each section and how they know. Visitors ask the check questions. Last, ask your child: 'How can you tell if something is alive?' and 'Was the dry bean alive?'

Which one is alive?
Which one was once alive?
A wooden table was once part of a…
Which of these can a living thing do, but a stone can't?
Living things need water, air and ____.
Match the mother to her baby.
Your child says, you write: How do you know a dog is alive? Give two clues.
Your child says, you write: Is a tree alive, even though a tree can't walk? Why?
Draw or write what you found at home or at the window.
Match each living thing to a sign of life you saw.
How does a plant move?
opts: by turning their leaves slowly towards the light

sections.p: How does a plant get their food?
opts: they make it in their green leaves, using sunlight

sections.p: Is it a plant or an animal? Both are alive.
A pigeon is sitting on eggs on a ledge. Which sign of life is that?
Your child says, you write: What did you find that was once alive? What living thing did it come from?
Your child says, you write: A toy car moves. Is it alive? Why not?
A dry seed doesn't move or eat. Is the seed alive?
opts: No, a seed is like a stone

sections.p: What woke up our soaked beans?
Why didn't the boiled beans grow?
opts: boiling killed the baby plant inside

sections.p: The balloon filled up because the ____ was alive. They ate the sugar and gave out a gas.
Is it alive, or is it a non-living thing that living things need?
Plastic is made from oil. Oil was made, over millions of years, from tiny living things in the sea. So plastic is…
opts: made from something that was once alive, long ago

sections.p: Your child says, you write: Is fire alive? Give one reason for yes and one for no.
Your child says, you write: How could you find out if a tiny brown seed in an old box is still alive?
Your child says, you write: An ant and an elephant. Is one of them more alive than the other? Why do you think so?

experiments.title: Wake the seeds
experiments.question: Is a dry seed alive?
need: 3 beans boiled for 10 minutes by a grown-up
steps: Cup A: the 3 soaked beans on damp cotton.
Cup B: 3 dry beans on dry cotton.
Cup C: the 3 boiled beans on damp cotton.
Keep A and C damp. Look every day for a week and draw.
On Day 6, move the dry beans onto damp cotton and watch them wake too.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which beans will grow? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: Which cups sprout. A white root pushes out of the soaked beans and grows down. The boiled beans go soft and never sprout.
experiments.why: A seed holds a baby plant and a store of food. A dry seed is alive but dormant. Water and warmth wake the seed, and they germinate: they use their stored food to grow a root and a shoot. Dry seeds stay dormant until they get water. Boiling kills the baby plant inside, so the bean can never grow.
experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the beans and lets them cool.

experiments.title: The balloon that blows itself up
experiments.question: Can something too tiny to see be alive?
need: half a cup of warm (not hot) water
steps: Put the yeast and sugar in the bottle.
Pour in the warm water and swirl.
Stretch the balloon over the neck of the bottle.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the balloon?'
experiments.observe: Bubbles in the bottle, and the balloon slowly filling up.
experiments.why: Yeast is millions of tiny living things, a kind of fungus. Dry yeast is dormant. Warm water wakes them. They eat the sugar and give out a gas called carbon dioxide, which fills the balloon. The same gas makes bread dough rise. If nothing happens, the water may have been too hot or the yeast too old: try again with fresh yeast.
experiments.safety: Use warm, not hot, water. Don't drink the mixture.

activities.title: Once-alive treasure hunt
steps: Your child walks round the house with a basket and collects (or names) 10 things that were once part of a living thing.
For each thing, your child says which living thing it came from: a tree, the cotton plant, a sheep, a silkworm, a bee, a coconut palm, the rice plant.
Lay them in a row with a paper label: 'from a tree', 'from a sheep'.
Count how many came from plants and how many from animals.
Look round the room. What here was never alive? (Glass, steel, stone.)
activities.outcome: A row of once-alive things, and the surprise that much of a home, and nearly all our food, was once alive.

project.title: My alive museum
steps: Find a tray and divide it into three sections with paper strips.

Collect 3 to 5 things for each section. Alive: a seedling from the seed cups, a small potted plant. Once alive: a feather, a dry leaf, a wooden peg, a piece of coconut shell. Never alive: a stone, a coin, a steel spoon.
Your child says a label for each, saying how they know, and you write it.
Give the family a museum tour.
project.outcome: A small museum and a child who can explain each object.

game.title: Alive or Not?
rules: Cut out the cards. Put the three heading cards (yellow) on the table.
Take turns picking a card and putting it under the right heading, saying why.
Others can challenge: 'I don't agree, because…'
Some cards are tricky on purpose. If you can't agree, make a fourth pile: 'We're not sure!'

cards.back: once alive (made by bees from flowers)
never alive (but made from oil, which formed from living things long ago)

big: A dry seed doesn't move or eat. How can a seed be alive?
Is a robot alive if it can move and talk?
Plastic is made from oil, and oil formed from tiny living things millions of years ago. So was plastic once alive?
Is a tiny ant just as alive as a big elephant, or a tree?
Tiny living things live inside you and help you digest food. Are they part of you?

challenge.q: People say living things are things that move. Is that right?
challenge.hint: A tree doesn't walk, and a dry seed doesn't move at all, but both are alive. A toy car moves but isn't alive. So moving is not enough to show something is alive.

challenge.q: Is it easy to tell what's alive?
challenge.hint: Not always. Scientists still argue about viruses: some say viruses are alive, some say they are not. NASA, which looks for life on other planets, had to write down what it means by 'alive' so it knows what to look for.

challenge.q: We call some plants 'weeds'. Are they less alive than the plants we grow?
challenge.hint: A weed is a plant growing where a person doesn't want it. A weed grows, drinks, makes food and makes seeds like any other plant. The word 'weed' tells you what people want, not anything about the plant.

perspectives.who: A dry seed in a jar
perspectives.view: A seed can stay dormant for years and still grow when rain comes. Waiting is how many plants survive dry times. Ask: why might it help a seed to wait for rain instead of growing straight away?

Many communities in India and around the world treat rivers, hills and forests as living beings to be respected, and in 2017 a law in New Zealand gave the Whanganui River the rights of a legal person. Ask: is a river alive? Why might people say so?
Earthworms eat dead leaves and turn them into soil that plants need. To a worm, a fallen leaf isn't rubbish, it's dinner. Ask: what would the garden be like with no worms?

Margulis argued that the energy-makers inside our cells, called mitochondria, were once free-living bacteria that came to live inside bigger cells. About fifteen journals turned her paper down before one printed it in 1967. Later, DNA evidence showed she was right. Ask: if parts of your cells were once bacteria, are those parts still alive?

voices.who: Sarah Sallon and Elaine Solowey, Israel (2005)
voices.idea: Sarah Sallon got some ancient date-palm seeds that archaeologists had found at Masada, an old desert fortress. Elaine Solowey, a plant scientist, soaked them, fed them and planted them. One sprouted. Scientists tested a piece of the seed's shell and found it was about 2,000 years old. They named the palm Methuselah.
voices.then: Many people thought a seed that old must be dead. Methuselah became one of the oldest seeds ever known to sprout.
voices.now: Methuselah is now a tall male palm who has made pollen, and the team has woken more ancient date seeds. Some seeds can stay alive and dormant for hundreds of years.
voices.ask: The seed was alive for 2,000 years, just dormant. Can something be alive and look completely dead? What else might be like that?

voices.idea: Van Leeuwenhoek sold cloth for a living and never went to university. He taught himself to grind tiny, powerful lenses, and in the 1670s he saw, in a drop of pond water and in scrapings from his own teeth, swarms of tiny moving creatures he called 'animalcules'.
voices.then: When he wrote to the Royal Society in London, the learned men there doubted him. They sent people to check, and eventually saw the creatures too.
voices.now: He was right. He was the first person to see bacteria and other microbes, tiny living things that are everywhere. He also saw yeast, the living thing in our balloon.
voices.ask: The experts doubted a cloth-seller with no degree. Why do you think they didn't believe him at first? How was he shown to be right?

story.title: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years
text: Long, long ago, on a high, hot hill in the desert, there was a great fortress, and in the fortress grew a date palm. Its dates were sweet and golden, and the people who lived there ate them and dropped the seeds, and some of the seeds fell into the cracks between the stones.
One small brown seed fell into a dark, dry crack and lay very still.

Inside the hard brown coat, the seed was alive. Curled up tight was a tiny baby palm, with a store of food beside them. But it was too dry to grow, so the seed did what seeds do. They rested. They didn't grow. They hardly breathed. They waited for rain.
But no rain came into that crack. Instead, there was a terrible war at the fortress, and then the people left, and the fortress was empty, and the wind blew sand over the stones.

A hundred years went by. Then five hundred. Kings and queens were born and died all over the world. People invented clocks, and ships that sailed around the Earth. The seed rested on in the dark, holding the tiny baby palm and the store of food, waiting.
One thousand years. Two thousand years. People invented trains, and aeroplanes, and phones.

Then one day, archaeologists came to the old fortress. They brushed away the sand very gently, looking for clues about the people who had lived there. And in a crack between the stones, they found some old, brown date seeds. They put them in a little box, and the box sat on a shelf for many more years.
Then a woman called Sarah, who studied plants as medicines, asked a question that nobody had asked before. "What if they're still alive?"
People laughed a little. Two thousand years! Surely the seeds were dead.
But Sarah took three seeds to her friend Elaine, who had a gift for growing difficult plants in the desert. Elaine looked at the old brown seeds in her palm. "Let's see," she said.
She soaked them in warm water, the first water they had touched in two thousand years. She gave them a little plant food. She planted them in fresh soil, and she watered them, and she waited.
Deep inside one of the seeds, something stirred. The water had found its way in. The baby palm, curled up for so long, began to use the stored food, and grew.
Eight weeks later, Elaine went to look at the pot. A small green shoot had pushed up through the soil.
She called Sarah. They stood together and looked at the shoot: a baby palm from a seed two thousand years old.
They named him Methuselah, after a very old man in an old story. Today Methuselah is taller than a grown-up, with long green leaves that rustle in the desert wind.
And in dark, dry places all over the world, other seeds are resting, and waiting, and alive.
story.epiphany: A seed is alive even when they show no signs of life: the seed is dormant, holding a baby plant and stored food, and water wakes them (germination). The turn is the green shoot pushing up after 2,000 years. Underneath: two women scientists who tried what others thought was pointless (based on the true story of Methuselah, who sprouted in 2005).
ask: What was inside the seed the whole time?
Why didn't the seed grow in the crack?
Why did people laugh at Sarah's question? Were they right?
Was the seed alive while it rested in the crack? How do you know?

ideas.more: Wood, cotton, paper, silk, wool, leather and shells were once part of living things. Look around: much of a house, and nearly all our food, was once alive.
Seeds and yeast can stay alive for years without growing, waiting for water. This resting is called being dormant.

ideas.idea: Plants and animals are both alive, and all life needs non-living things.
ideas.more: Animals eat food and move about. Plants make their own food and move slowly towards light. Both grow, breathe and make young. Both need water and air, which are not alive.

unknowns: How long can a seed stay dormant and still grow? Date seeds about 2,000 years old have sprouted. Nobody knows the limit.
What exactly makes something alive? Scientists still argue, especially about viruses.
How many kinds of living things are there on Earth? Nobody knows; most tiny ones have never been named.

books.title: A Seed Is Sleepy
books.author: Dianna Hutts Aston
books.why: Exactly this idea: seeds rest, wait and wake.

books.title: What's Alive?
books.author: Kathleen Weidner Zoehfeld
books.why: A Let's-Read-and-Find-Out book that compares living and non-living things simply and well.

books.title: Living Sunlight: How Plants Bring the Earth to Life
books.author: Molly Bang and Penny Chisholm
books.why: The Sun tells how sunlight becomes plants, food and every living thing, including us.

check.q: Name something alive, something once alive and something never alive.
check.a: For example, a cat, a wooden spoon and a stone.
They grow, need food, water and air, breathe, move or respond, and make young.

check.q: Is a dry seed alive? How do we know?
check.a: Yes. The seed was dormant. When we gave the bean water, the bean germinated and grew.

check.q: Why did the balloon fill up?
check.a: The yeast is alive. The yeast ate the sugar and gave out a gas.

check.q: Is a tree alive, even though a tree can't walk?
check.a: Yes. A tree grows, drinks, makes food, breathes and makes seeds.

check.q: Name two things in your house that were once alive, and what they came from.
check.a: For example, a cotton shirt from the cotton plant, and a wooden door from a tree.

check.q: What do all living things need?
check.a: Water, air and food. Plants make their food using sunlight.
